about: The work people do in a settlement, by what the place lives by (trades), the land around it (terrains), its water and its size: who does it (an Orsino background, so that one who has done the same work knows them for one of their own), where it is done and what that place is like, what they are seen doing there, what they say of it when asked, and the painting (data/paintings) that hangs beside them in conversation. A line's {Name} is the worker; {they} {their} the words they are spoken of in; {place} the settlement. An occupation with foundings is the work of settlements founded so (see foundings.json), and is taken there first.
evening: {Name} is at the long table with a cup, telling a long story about a horse.
{Name} is by the fire with {their} boots off and {their} feet to the warmth, half asleep.
{Name} is playing at dice in the corner, and losing, and laughing about it.
{Name} is eating mutton stew from a wooden bowl.
{Name} is arguing with the next table about the price of wool.

recognition.wild: {Name} looks at your boots, and then at your hands. 'You've worked the hills,' {they} [say|says]. 'You'll want to know which way the weather comes from here. West. Always west.' {They} [press|presses] a heel of bread on you for the road.
recognition.roads: 'You've walked a few roads,' says {Name}, not as a question. 'Here: the inn at the far end is better than the near one. Tell them I sent you.' {They} [give|gives] you a twist of dried meat for the way.
recognition.water: {Name} watches you tie a knot and nods, slowly. 'Boat people,' {they} [say|says]. 'You can always tell.' {They} [hand|hands] you a smoked fish wrapped in a dock leaf.
recognition.trade: 'You've done honest work,' says {Name}. {They} [give|gives] you bread and a piece of cheese for the road.
recognition.earth: 'Dug, have you?' says {Name}, and grips your hand to feel the calluses. 'Thought so.' {They} [give|gives] you a hard cake of oats, the kind that keeps underground.
recognition.faith: {Name} sees how you hold yourself and lowers {their} voice. 'Bless you,' {they} [say|says], and gives you bread.
recognition.healing: 'You've the hands of someone who's set a bone,' says {Name}. 'Here. Take this for the road.'
recognition.learning: 'You read,' says {Name}, surprised, when you make out the mark on the door-post. 'Then you'll want to know the old stones say more than people think.' {They} [give|gives] you an oatcake while {they} [talk|talks].
recognition.arms: {Name} sizes you up the way soldiers do. 'Who'd you serve with?' {They} [don't|doesn't] wait for an answer, but presses some food on you all the same.
recognition.stage: 'I've seen you somewhere,' says {Name}. 'A fair. You played.' {They} [laugh|laughs] and gives you a heel of bread for the memory of it.
recognition.shadows: {Name} looks at you a moment too long. 'I know your sort,' {they} [say|says], not unkindly. 'Keep out of the reeve's way and you'll do.' {They} [give|gives] you bread, and counts the spoons when you have gone.
recognition.court: {Name} straightens without meaning to. 'You've been in great houses,' {they} [say|says]. 'You'll find this one plainer.' {They} [give|gives] you bread anyway.
recognition.mechanisms: 'You've a clever pair of hands,' says {Name}, watching you. 'If you're staying, there's a lock at the mill wants looking at.' {They} [give|gives] you a heel of bread in the meantime.
recognition.margins: {Name} knows what you are, and does not say it, and gives you bread without being asked.

farmer.name: farmer

workplace.name: the home fields
workplace.scene: Strips of field run out from the backs of the houses, each a different green, with a headland of nettles between.

seen: {Name} is walking a strip of barley, pulling charlock.
{Name} is laying a gap in a hedge with a billhook.
{Name} is leaning on a gate, looking at a field of beans gone black with fly.
{Name} is carrying a lamb under each arm across the yard, the ewe following.
talk: 'It wants rain and it wants sun, and never both at once,' says {Name}. 'Same as every year. We'll eat.'
'The far strip floods,' says {Name}. 'My father's father dug a ditch for it. I keep it open. That's farming: keeping somebody else's ditch open.'

smith.name: smith

workplace.name: the smithy
workplace.scene: A low smithy, open on the street side, dark inside but for the forge. Horseshoes hang on a nail by the door in a long grey string.

seen: {Name} is drawing out a bar on the anvil, the hammer going like a clock.
{Name} is quenching a hinge-strap in the trough, and does not look up.
{Name} is working the bellows with one hand and eating bread with the other.
{Name} is holding a horseshoe up to the light, then putting it back in the fire.
talk: 'Hinges and nails and horseshoes,' says {Name}. 'Everybody wants a sword till they see what a sword costs, then they want a better hinge.'
'Bring me good iron and I'll make you anything,' says {Name}. 'Bring me bad iron and I'll make you a lesson.'

carpenter.name: carpenter

workplace.name: the wright's yard
workplace.scene: A yard of stacked timber under a lean-to, with sawdust underfoot and a half-made cart on trestles.

seen: {Name} is cutting a mortise, a chisel in one hand and the mallet in the other, a pencil behind one ear.
{Name} is sighting along a plank with one eye shut, looking for the warp.
{Name} is planing a board, the shavings curling up round {their} boots.
{Name} is measuring a doorway with a knotted string.
talk: 'Oak for the frame, ash for the shafts, elm for anything that stays wet,' says {Name}. 'People think it's all just wood.'
'Half the doors in {place} are mine,' says {Name}. 'The other half stick.'

baker.name: baker

workplace.name: the bakehouse
workplace.scene: A bakehouse, hot as summer, with a long peel on the wall and flour on every ledge.

seen: {Name} is drawing loaves out of the oven on the long peel, quick and careful.
{Name} is kneading a trough of dough with both fists, up to the elbow in it.
{Name} is sitting on a flour sack by the oven door, cooling {their} face in the street air.
{Name} is scoring the tops of the loaves with a knife.
talk: 'Up at three,' says {Name}. 'Every day of my life. You get used to it, they tell me. They're liars.'
'The miller sends the flour,' says {Name}, 'and I send it back a loaf at a time. Neither of us is paid enough.'

brewer.name: alewife
seen: {Name} is rolling a cask along the street, steering it with one foot.
{Name} is tasting the new ale from a dipper.
{Name} is stirring a vat with a paddle as long as an oar, in a cloud of sweet steam.
{Name} is knocking on each cask in a row, listening for the empty ones.
talk: 'The inn takes all I brew and complains of all of it,' says {Name}. 'That's how I know it's good.'
'Water, barley, a bit of luck,' says {Name}. 'And the barley's not what it was.'

weaver.name: weaver

workplace.name: the weaving shed
workplace.scene: A long shed with two looms in it and hanks of yarn hung from the beams to dry, browns and duns and one startling blue.

seen: {Name} is at the loom, throwing the shuttle.
{Name} is winding yarn off a skein held between two chair backs.
{Name} is carrying a bolt of cloth out into the daylight to look at the colour.
{Name} is untangling a skein of brown wool.
talk: 'The blue's woad, from the other side of the hills,' says {Name}. 'Dear as silver. The rest is what the sheep came with.'
'A cloak a week, if I am left alone at the loom,' says {Name}.

shepherd.name: shepherd

workplace.name: the sheepfold
workplace.scene: A stone fold on the edge of the settlement, its walls dry-laid and its gate a hurdle tied with twine.

seen: {Name} is going through the flock with a crook, looking at each ewe's teeth.
{Name} is sitting on the fold wall with a dog at {their} feet, watching the flock.
{Name} is carrying a lame ewe across {their} shoulders.
{Name} is whistling the dog round the far side of the flock, two notes, and the dog goes.
talk: 'Lost two to the crows this spring and one to a crag,' says {Name}. 'Sheep are always looking for a new way to die.'
'The dog does the work,' says {Name}. 'I'm just here to tell her she's clever.'

cowherd.name: cowherd

workplace.name: the byre
workplace.scene: A byre of black timber, warm, with a row of broad backs in the gloom and a smell of hay and dung.

seen: {Name} is forking hay to the cows.
{Name} is leaning on the byre door, chewing a stem of grass.
{Name} is walking the cows down the lane with a hazel stick.
{Name} is milking on a three-legged stool, {their} forehead against the cow's flank.
talk: 'Six cows,' says {Name}, 'and every one of them knows the way home better than I do.'
'Milk, butter, cheese, and a calf in spring if we're lucky,' says {Name}. 'Cows don't argue. That's why I like them.'

goose_girl.name: goose-girl
seen: {Name} is driving a gaggle of geese between the houses with a willow switch.
{Name} is sitting on an upturned basket with the geese round {their} feet.
{Name} is counting the geese through a gap in a fence.
{Name} is flapping an apron at a hissing gander on the path.
talk: 'They bite,' says {Name}. 'Mind your ankles. That big one bites priests.'
'Feathers for the fletchers, eggs for the inn, and one for the reeve at Michaelmas,' says {Name}. 'He never gets the biggest.'

eel_catcher.name: eel-catcher

workplace.name: the eel-weirs
workplace.scene: Wicker eel-traps are stacked on the bank to dry, and a flat-bottomed boat lies drawn up beside them, green to the gunwale.

seen: {Name} is mending an eel-trap with a willow withy.
{Name} is gutting eels on a board, and a heron waits a little way off for the leavings.
{Name} is setting traps in the shallows, feeling for the bottom with bare feet.
{Name} is carrying a dripping basket of live eels.
talk: 'Eels run in the dark of the moon,' says {Name}. 'Light nights, you might as well sleep.'
'Nobody knows where eels breed,' says {Name}. 'They come up the river in spring no thicker than a bootlace.'

fisher.name: fisher
seen: {Name} is sitting on the bank with a line in the water and an empty creel.
{Name} is spreading a net over a wall to dry.
{Name} is gutting the morning's catch on an upturned boat, with gulls waiting round it.
{Name} is baiting hooks along a long line with lugworm.
talk: 'Trout in the pools, if you're quiet,' says {Name}. 'Nobody's quiet.'
'The water knows more than you'd think,' says {Name}. 'It brings things down. I've had a boot, a door and a sheep, and the sheep was alive.'

reed_cutter.name: reed-cutter

workplace.name: the reed-beds
workplace.scene: The reed comes right up to the last houses, with paths cut into it and bundles stacked in ricks on the hard ground.

seen: {Name} is binding a bundle of reed with a twist of itself, and stacking it on the rick.
{Name} is up to the knees in water, cutting reed with a sickle.
{Name} is loading reed onto a flat-bottomed boat.
{Name} is sitting on a bundle of reed, putting an edge on a sickle with a whetstone.
talk: 'Best reed is winter reed,' says {Name}. 'Cut it when your hands are too cold to feel the sickle. That's how you know.'
'Every roof from here to the hills is our reed,' says {Name}. 'You've slept under some of it, I'd bet.'

thatcher.name: thatcher
seen: {Name} is up a ladder against a roof, beating reed into place with a wooden bat.
{Name} is sorting spars on the ground, splitting hazel with a hook.
{Name} is shouting down from a roof for more spars.
{Name} is combing out a bundle of straw with {their} fingers, pulling the short stems.
talk: 'A good roof lasts longer than the man who made it,' says {Name}. 'A bad one lasts longer than his good name.'
'Mind the eaves,' says {Name}. 'I'm not paid to catch anyone.'

salt_boiler.name: salt-boiler

workplace.name: the salt-pans
workplace.scene: Low sheds over shallow lead pans, fires under them, and white steam going up off the brine. The ground is crusted grey and crunches.

seen: {Name} is raking salt to the edge of a pan and lifting it out with a wooden scoop.
{Name} is feeding the fire under a pan with peat, coughing in the steam.
{Name} is carrying a basket of wet salt to the drying house.
{Name} is skimming scum off a pan with a wooden paddle, {their} eyes streaming.
talk: 'Brine in, fire under, salt out,' says {Name}. 'Sounds easy. Try it with wet peat.'
'The whole country eats our salt,' says {Name}, 'and we get the coughs.'

peat_cutter.name: peat-cutter
seen: {Name} is stacking turves to dry, three leaning on one.
{Name} is cleaning a long narrow spade, the turf-iron, with a handful of grass.
{Name} is cutting turves out of the bank with a long spade.
{Name} is wheeling a barrow of dry peats along a plank laid over the bog.
talk: 'You cut it in spring and burn it in winter,' says {Name}. 'If you cut it in winter you'll burn it in spring and freeze in winter.'
'Things come up out of the moss,' says {Name}. 'A butter-keg once. A wooden spoon. A hand, my uncle said. He drank.'

woodcutter.name: woodcutter
seen: {Name} is splitting logs on a block, each one in two strokes.
{Name} is sharpening an axe on a wheel, testing the edge on {their} thumbnail.
{Name} is resting on the axe-helve, looking up at an oak marked for felling.
{Name} is dragging a lopped branch along behind {them}, leaves and all.
talk: 'Oak for the wrights, ash for the wheel, birch for the fire,' says {Name}. 'And hazel for everything else.'
'You don't go into the old wood without leave,' says {Name}. 'Not leave from the reeve. Leave.'

charcoal_burner.name: charcoal-burner

workplace.name: the charcoal clamps
workplace.scene: Two domed clamps of turf smoke on a cleared floor beyond the houses. The air tastes of tar. A hut of poles and bracken stands by them.

seen: {Name} is walking round a smoking clamp, stopping where the smoke comes thickest.
{Name} is asleep sitting up by the clamp, black to the eyes.
{Name} is patching a clamp with turf where the smoke has found a way out.
{Name} is raking charcoal out into sacks, black and light as cinders.
talk: 'A clamp burns five days,' says {Name}. 'You sit up with it like a sick child. Let it flare and you've made ash.'
'The smiths want it, the salters want it,' says {Name}. 'Nobody wants a charcoal-burner in the house.'

beekeeper.name: beekeeper

workplace.name: the bee-garden
workplace.scene: A walled garden of herbs and old fruit trees, with straw skeps along the south wall in niches. The air hums.

seen: {Name} is bent over a skep, telling the bees the news in a low voice.
{Name} is pressing comb in a cloth bag, honey running out of it in a thread.
{Name} is walking slowly among the hives with a smoking pot, and the bees let {them} by.
{Name} is picking a bee out of {their} hair.
talk: 'You tell them things,' says {Name}. 'Births, deaths, weddings. They take offence if you don't. I told them about you.'
'Wax for the shrine, honey for the inn, mead for the reeve,' says {Name}. 'Stings for me.'

chandler.name: candle-maker
seen: {Name} is dipping a rack of wicks into a tub of tallow.
{Name} is trimming a candle with a knife, and lighting it to see.
{Name} is hanging new candles in pairs along a rail to harden.
{Name} is skimming a pot of tallow, and the whole street smells of it.
talk: 'Tallow for the houses, wax for the shrine,' says {Name}. 'The gods like the good stuff.'
'Every light in {place} after dark is mine,' says {Name}. 'Think of that when you're reading.'

quarrier.name: quarrier

workplace.name: the quarry
workplace.scene: A quarry face of blue-grey slate rises behind the settlement, with ledges cut into it and heaps of spoil below.

seen: {Name} is splitting slate into roofing sheets with a broad chisel.
{Name} is sitting on a heap of spoil eating bread and onion, grey to the eyebrows.
{Name} is driving wedges into a crack in the rock, a tap on each in turn.
{Name} is levering a block along on rollers, an inch at a time.
talk: 'Every roof in three valleys,' says {Name}. 'Slate keeps the rain off and lasts forever. Which is bad for business.'
'The old face is closed,' says {Name}. 'Something in the rock. You hit it and it rings. Nobody likes the note.'

miner.name: miner

workplace.name: the mine-head
workplace.scene: The black mouth of an adit in the hillside, with a little wooden frame over it, a pile of ore beside, and water running out of it orange.

seen: {Name} is coming up out of the adit with a basket of ore on {their} back, blinking.
{Name} is washing ore in a sluice, picking through the grit with quick fingers.
{Name} is sitting at the adit mouth trimming a lamp, with the dark at {their} back.
{Name} is sharpening picks on a stone, one after another, and trying each with a thumb.
talk: 'Dark, wet and low,' says {Name}. 'And that's the good level.'
'The old people had the tin first,' says {Name}. 'We keep breaking into their workings. Their props are better than ours.'

smelter.name: smelter
seen: {Name} is pumping a bellows with a foot, slow and steady, watching the colour of the fire.
{Name} is pouring a little bright run of tin into a mould, holding {their} breath.
{Name} is breaking ore to the size of peas on a stone with a hammer.
{Name} is raking slag out of the furnace mouth, {their} face turned away from the heat.
talk: 'Tin and copper, nine to one,' says {Name}. 'Get it wrong and the bell rings flat. Everyone knows whose fault it is.'

trapper.name: trapper
seen: {Name} is stretching a pelt on a frame of withies, scraping it with a blade.
{Name} is oiling a row of snares and laying them out in order.
{Name} is skinning a marten on a bench with a small knife.
{Name} is sorting pelts into piles by the thickness of the fur.
talk: 'Marten, fox, beaver if you know the water,' says {Name}. 'Wolf if the wolf is careless, which is never.'
'You learn a beast by its road,' says {Name}. 'Same as people. They all go home the same way.'

furrier.name: furrier
seen: {Name} is sewing a collar of grey fur with tiny stitches, the needle going in and out of sight.
{Name} is blowing into a pelt to see the colour at the root.
{Name} is brushing a fur cape against the lie and then with it, to watch it shine.
{Name} is matching pelts for a cape on a table, turning them to the light.
talk: 'A good pelt is winter-caught,' says {Name}. 'Summer fur sheds in your hands. People try to sell me summer fur. People are fools.'

whaler.name: whaler

workplace.name: the try-works
workplace.scene: On the shore below the houses, great iron pots on stone hearths, black with use, and the ribs of a whale bleaching beside them on the shingle.

seen: {Name} is scraping a try-pot clean with a long iron.
{Name} is coiling a line on the shingle, looking out to sea.
{Name} is putting an edge on a long flensing knife, and the steel sings on the stone.
{Name} is sitting under an arch of whale's jawbone, splicing a rope.
talk: 'One whale lights the country for a winter,' says {Name}. 'We go out for three and come back with one and are glad of it.'
'The big ones talk,' says {Name}. 'Under the boat. You feel it in your teeth.'

ice_cutter.name: ice-cutter
seen: {Name} is sawing a block out of the ice with a long-toothed saw, and the water under it is black.
{Name} is loading blocks of ice onto a sledge, wrapped in straw.
{Name} is scoring a line on the ice with an iron, measuring it out with {their} feet.
{Name} is stamping {their} feet and blowing on {their} hands between strokes of the saw.
talk: 'The ice-house keeps it till midsummer,' says {Name}. 'Then the reeve has cold beer and the rest of us have chilblains.'

herbwife.name: herb-wife
seen: {Name} is hanging bunches of sage to dry from a line under the eaves.
{Name} is grinding willow bark in a stone mortar.
{Name} is stripping leaves off a stem into a basket, smelling each handful.
{Name} is tying up a twist of paper with thread and marking it with charcoal.
talk: 'Yarrow for a cut, feverfew for the head, willow bark for a fever,' says {Name}. 'The willow grows by water, if you want to know. Everything good does.'
'I've nothing left,' says {Name}. 'Half {place} has had the cough. If you're going anywhere damp, bring me back what grows there.'

midwife.name: midwife
seen: {Name} is sitting in a doorway in the sun with {their} eyes shut, catching up on a night.
{Name} is washing linen in a tub, sleeves rolled to the shoulder.
{Name} is walking quickly up the street with a bag, the way people walk when they are wanted.
{Name} is drinking hot broth on a bench, both hands round the cup.
talk: 'Every soul in {place} under forty, I caught,' says {Name}. 'I don't let them forget it.'
'Up all night with the Hayward child,' says {Name}. 'A girl. Loud. She'll do.'

reeve.name: reeve
seen: {Name} is reading a notice nailed to a post, lips moving.
{Name} is counting sacks into a cart, making marks on a tally-stick with a knife.
{Name} is pacing out a boundary along a hedge, counting under {their} breath.
{Name} is hearing out two neighbours' quarrel at a gate.
talk: 'Somebody has to say whose turn it is to clear the ditch,' says {Name}. 'That's me. I'm much loved for it.'
'The lord's man comes at quarter-day for the rents,' says {Name}. 'And for anything else he can find. Keep your head down when he's here.'

sexton.name: sexton
seen: {Name} is sweeping the shrine step, slowly, every corner.
{Name} is trimming the grass round the graves with shears, kneeling.
{Name} is digging, steadily, down past {their} knees, and does not stop to look up.
{Name} is oiling the hinges of the shrine door.
talk: 'I ring the bell and dig the graves,' says {Name}. 'Beginning and end. The priest does the middle.'
'Old dead don't trouble me,' says {Name}. 'It's the new ones who want looking after.'

tinker.name: tinker
seen: {Name} is sitting at the side of the way mending a pot, with {their} wares spread on a blanket.
{Name} is crying wares along the street: pots mended, knives ground.
{Name} is soldering a hole in a kettle over a little fire, squinting through the smoke.
{Name} is grinding a knife on a treadle wheel, sending sparks into the dust.
talk: 'I go round,' says {Name}. 'Here a week, gone a month. You'd be surprised what people tell a tinker. You'd be surprised what a tinker tells.'
'Knives ground, pots mended, and no questions,' says {Name}. 'I ask the questions.'

laundress.name: laundress
seen: {Name} is beating linen on a flat stone by the water, and the sound carries.
{Name} is spreading shirts on a hedge to dry.
{Name} and a girl are wringing out a sheet between them, twisting it like a rope.
{Name} is carrying a basket of wet washing on {their} hip, up the street at a slant.
talk: 'You can tell everything about a house by its washing,' says {Name}. 'Everything. I'll not say what.'

schoolmaster.name: schoolmaster
seen: {Name} is sitting in a doorway with a slate on {their} knee and three children at {their} feet.
{Name} is reading a book while walking.
{Name} is writing letters in the dust with a stick for a small child.
{Name} is cutting a new nib on a goose-quill with a penknife.
talk: 'I teach letters and figures to anyone who'll sit still,' says {Name}. 'Two, this year.'
'The old script? I can read a little,' says {Name}. 'Enough to know when it's a warning.'

fiddler.name: fiddler
seen: {Name} is tuning a fiddle on a bench, frowning at one string.
{Name} is playing a slow air on the fiddle, eyes shut.
{Name} is rosining a bow, and trying the same three notes over and over.
{Name} is asleep on a bench with the fiddle in {their} lap.
talk: 'Weddings, wakes and the inn on a market night,' says {Name}. 'Same tunes for all three, a bit faster for the weddings.'
'I know a song about every place in this country,' says {Name}. 'Most of them are rude.'

old_soldier.name: old soldier
seen: {Name} is sitting on a bench in the sun with one leg straight out in front of {them}, watching the road.
{Name} is cleaning an old pike-head with sand and spit.
{Name} is telling some children about a siege.
{Name} is marching up and down outside the door, to keep the knee from stiffening.
talk: 'I was in the lord's muster when the river burned,' says {Name}. 'Don't ask me about it.' A pause. 'All right. Sit down.'
'You want to know how to fight?' says {Name}. 'Don't. Next question.'

carter.name: carter
seen: {Name} is greasing a cart-axle with a rag.
{Name} is roping down a load of barrels.
{Name} is backing a cart into a yard, one hand on the horse's bridle.
{Name} is going round the cart wheel by wheel, a kick and a look at each.
talk: 'Every road in the country, I've had a wheel off on,' says {Name}. 'Ask me which. Go on.'
'The road's all right,' says {Name}. 'It's the people on it. And the weather. And the road.'

ferryman.name: ferry-keeper
seen: {Name} sits on the bank by the crossing with a pole across {their} knees, watching the water.
{Name} is wading out to fetch back a marker post the river has moved in the night.
{Name} is bailing out the ferry with a wooden scoop.
{Name} is counting coins into a leather bag, and then counting them again.
talk: 'Most days you can walk it,' says {Name}. 'Some days you can't, and those are the days people try.'
'I've pulled eleven out of that water,' says {Name}. 'Twelve, if you count the bishop, and he'd want you to.'

boatwright.name: boatwright
seen: {Name} is steaming a plank in a long box to bend it.
{Name} is sighting along a keel with one eye shut.
{Name} is caulking a seam along the boat's side with oakum and a mallet.
{Name} is running a hand along a new-cut plank, feeling for the grain.
talk: 'A boat's only a box that wants to be wet,' says {Name}. 'The trick is stopping it wanting to be full.'
'Oak for the keel, larch for the planks, and patience for the rest,' says {Name}. 'Nobody sells the last.'

net_maker.name: net-maker
seen: {Name} is knotting a net with a wooden needle.
{Name} has a net spread over three fences and is walking along it, looking for holes.
{Name} is soaking a finished net in a tub of bark-brown water.
{Name} is measuring a mesh against two fingers.
talk: 'A net's mostly holes,' says {Name}. 'It's which holes that matters.'
'They tear it, I mend it, they tear it,' says {Name}. 'Seals, mostly.'

miller.name: miller
seen: {Name} is white with flour from the hair down, shouting up the stairs over the noise of the stones.
{Name} is dressing a millstone with a pick.
{Name} is hauling a sack up into the mill on a rope and a wheel, hand over hand.
{Name} is standing in the mill door, watching the level of the stream.
talk: 'Everyone thinks the miller cheats,' says {Name}. 'Everyone was right about the last one. Not me.'
'When the stream's low the stones go slow, and so does everything in the village,' says {Name}. 'You can tell a dry year by the bread.'

lay_brother.name: lay brother
seen: {Name} is sweeping the gate-yard.
{Name} is hoeing between rows of cabbages, saying the hours under {their} breath.
{Name} is ringing the small bell for the noon office.
{Name} is carrying two buckets up from the well, and stopping halfway to look at the sky.
talk: 'The brothers pray and we dig,' says {Name}. 'Some days I think we've got the better of it.'
'We're to be silent before the noon bell,' says {Name}, 'which it isn't, quite, so I'll be quick.'

soldier.name: soldier of the garrison
seen: {Name} is leaning on a spear in the shade of the wall, watching the road.
{Name} is polishing a dented helmet with sand.
{Name} is dicing on a drumhead with another, and losing.
{Name} is sharpening a sword on a whetstone.
talk: 'Nothing has come up the pass since the thaw,' says {Name}. 'That's the job: making sure nothing does.'
'Pay's late, beer's thin, and the sergeant's my uncle,' says {Name}. 'Could be worse. Could be the other side.'

stonemason.name: stonemason
seen: {Name} is fitting a new stone into a gap in an old wall.
{Name} is running a hand over the old paving, feeling the joints.
{Name} is dressing a block with a chisel, the chips flying, a cloth tied over {their} mouth.
{Name} is mixing lime mortar in a trough, a little water at a time.
talk: 'We can't cut stone like that,' says {Name}, nodding at the old work. 'Nobody can. I've tried.'
'The well's dressed stone all the way down,' says {Name}. 'I've been down forty steps. My father went sixty. Nobody's been to the bottom.'
